title: Smallest Number of Taps to Open to Water a Garden

notes: A tap contributes an interval clipped to the garden [0,n].
The goal is to cover the entire continuous interval [0,n] using the minimum number of tap intervals.

content.problemStatement:
There is a one-dimensional garden on the x-axis. The garden starts at the point `0` and ends at the point `n`. (i.e., the length of the garden is `n`).

There are `n + 1` taps located at points `[0, 1, ..., n]` in the garden.

With an integer `n` and an integer array `ranges` of length `n + 1` where `ranges[i]` (0-indexed) means the `i-th` tap can water the area `[i - ranges[i], i + ranges[i]]` if it was open.

Output *the smallest number of taps* that should be open to water the whole garden, If the garden cannot be watered output **-1**.

**Example 1:**

![](https://assets.leetcode.com/uploads/2020/01/16/1685_example_1.png)

```
Input: n = 5, ranges = [3,4,1,1,0,0]
Output: 1
Explanation: The tap at point 0 can cover the interval [-3,3]
The tap at point 1 can cover the interval [-3,5]
The tap at point 2 can cover the interval [1,3]
The tap at point 3 can cover the interval [2,4]
The tap at point 4 can cover the interval [4,4]
The tap at point 5 can cover the interval [5,5]
Opening Only the second tap will water the whole garden [0,5]
```

**Example 2:**

```
Input: n = 3, ranges = [0,0,0,0]
Output: -1
Explanation: Even if you activate all the four taps you cannot water the whole garden.
```

**Constraints:**

* `1 <= n <= 10^4`
* `ranges.length == n + 1`
* `0 <= ranges[i] <= 10000`

notes: Implement minTaps(n, ranges) and return the minimum number of taps, or -1 when [0,n] cannot be fully covered.
The clipping is only for the garden boundaries; coverage outside [0,n] is irrelevant.
The greedy choice is optimal because among all intervals that can extend the current covered prefix, choosing the one with the farthest right endpoint never reduces future options.
solution.approach: Convert each tap into its covered interval [max(0, i-ranges[i]), min(n, i+ranges[i])]. For every possible interval start, keep the farthest right endpoint available from that start. This turns the problem into a minimum-jump interval-cover problem. Scan from left to right while maintaining the farthest point reachable with the taps considered so far; whenever the current selected reach is exhausted, commit to one tap and extend to the farthest reachable endpoint. If the farthest endpoint cannot advance, the garden cannot be fully watered.

better.description: Use dynamic programming over reachable positions. After converting taps to intervals, compute the minimum number of intervals needed to reach each position by considering every tap interval that can start from an already-reachable position. This removes subset enumeration but still examines many interval/position combinations.

optimal.description: Convert each tap to a clipped interval and store the farthest right endpoint available for each left endpoint. Then use the classic minimum-jumps greedy sweep: currentEnd is the right boundary covered by the selected taps, and farthest is the best boundary reachable from all intervals whose left endpoint is within the current covered prefix. When the scan reaches currentEnd, select one more tap and set currentEnd to farthest. If the scan ever moves beyond farthest, a gap exists and the answer is -1.

bruteForce.complexity: O(2^n · n) time and O(n) auxiliary space.
bruteForce.description: Treat every tap as either open or closed and enumerate subsets, checking whether the union of the chosen intervals continuously covers [0,n]. This is useful only for very small n and serves as a correctness oracle for testing.

followUps: Why does choosing the farthest-reaching interval among currently usable taps minimize the number of taps?
What changes if n is much larger and the ranges are sparse?
Can the same greedy idea be expressed directly using the tap intervals without building the max-range array?
